    Jayapal Defies Trump with Secret Cuba Oil Plan

    TOPICS:cubaJayapalPatriot Newswire

    Posted By: KM Broussard May 11, 2026

    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 2:02
    Instaread

    Rep Pramila Jayapal just dropped a bombshell. The congresswoman admitted she held talks with Mexican and Latin American diplomats about ways to rush oil into Cuba. This Jayapal effort comes right after President Trump slapped tough sanctions on any nation helping the island. Yet her move has patriots across America fuming. 

    Jayapal’s Cuba Trip Fuels Controversy

    In early April 2026 Jayapal led a group to Havana. She met Cuban leaders and called the U.S. fuel limits cruel and illegal. Meanwhile shortages there have caused blackouts and hospital chaos. Jayapal returned home and pushed the story hard. However, her words now raise serious questions about crossing the line.

    Jayapal Admits Ambassador Talks on Oil

    At a Seattle briefing in early May Jayapal spoke plainly. She said she discussed oil deliveries with ambassadors from Mexico and other countries. Trump had warned of tariffs on any supplier. Still Jayapal described the situation as a humanitarian crisis. Therefore, she urged action to ease the pain in Cuba. This Jayapal push ignores the regime’s long record of trouble.

    Book Beach Resorts

    Jayapal Introduces Bill Against Cuba Action

    Jayapal also backed a new bill. It blocks federal money for any military move against Cuba without Congress approval. She tied the measure directly to the oil squeeze. Meanwhile Republicans blast the whole episode as defiance of clear U.S. policy. Critics even mention the Logan Act though no charges have surfaced yet. Jayapal insists it is simply congressional work.

    Book Beach Resorts

    Backlash Grows Over Jayapal Moves

    Republicans in the House demand answers fast. They call the outreach a direct challenge to Trump’s executive orders. Yet Jayapal stands firm and labels the sanctions an economic attack. The episode highlights deep splits on Cuba policy. Americans watch closely as fuel tankers remain rare and shortages continue. This Jayapal controversy lays bare the tension between humanitarian claims and strong national security steps. It leaves one key question: Should elected officials face real limits when they work to soften American sanctions?
